Definition: Diversification refers to growing multiple foods under multiple conditions to reduce the risk that any one hazard (e.g., hail, flood, or drought) will destroy the entire agricultural production in an area. Diversification strategies include diversifying what is grown, where it is grown, and when it is grown. It also includes diversifying by raising animals as well as plants, and by incorporating wild foods into the diet as well.

Ethnographic analogy is using ethnographic study of a contemporary human society to make inferences about the beliefs and practices of a society in the past who are no longer observable directly. This is considered stronger when using a group as the ethnographic case who are a good technological and ecological parallel for a past society: for example, the ethnographic study of Marsh Arabs who inhabited the swampy areas of the Tigris and Euphrates Rivers of southern Iraq provided valuable insights into how ancient Sumerians inhabited similar landscapes in southern Iraq thousands of years earlier.

Famine foods, or fallback foods, are those foods (usually wild plants and animals) that can be eaten but are not preferred, such that they are only eaten when no preferred, regularly eaten foods are available. These are often less nutritious or palatable, or much less efficient to prepare, requiring additional labor to make edible.

Food security is defined by the FAO as “when all people, at all times, have physical, social, and economic access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food that meets their dietary needs and food preferences for an healthy and active life.” It is the opposite of food insecurity.

Polarization describes the phenomenon in which waves of light can be restricted to a single plane of movement or oscillation. Since light can be described as a wave, polarized light is light in which the waves are limited to one and only one plane.

Agricultural scarcity is a term used by archaeologists to refer to crop yields that fall below a desired minimum threshold needed to provide immediate food supplies and, through storage, sufficient supplies for an uncertain future.
Secondary electrons are produced when the scanning electron beam sweeps over a conductive surface. They provide topographical information about the surface of the sample being analyzed.
Stereomicroscopes are reflected light microscopes with two optical pathways, one of which reaches each eye. This allows greater depth perception of the sample than a single eyepiece design.
